newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain, Ireland, assail death threat on Wright.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Ireland, assail death threat on Wright.

text.p: Britain and Ireland hinted on Tuesday that militant Protestant groups could face expulsion from Northern Ireland peace talks because of a death threat against maverick "Loyalist" Billy Wright.
"There is absolutely no place for this kind of threat in political discourse," Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told reporters six days before the peace talks resume in Belfast.

His words were echoed in an article in the Belfast Telgraph newspaper by Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, who said all participants in the peace talks had to abide by principles of non-violence.

The two governments were commenting on a death threat against Wright by the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), the umbrella group for Protestant guerrilla groups fighting to keep Northern Ireland British.

They are represented at the peace talks by the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) and Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), two fringe groups allowed to take part in the talks because of a ceasefire the CLMC called in October 1994.

Mayhew pointed out that Sinn Fein, the political arm of IRA guerrillas fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, were excluded from the talks because of the guerrillas' failure to renew a ceasefire they broke in February.
"Sinn Fein could not, despite their political mandate, participate in the talks without an IRA ceasefire being first in place," he wrote.
"It would be equally unacceptable for Loyalist parties to be at the talks had they not made the total and absolute commitment to the principes of democracy and on-violence."

Wright, who has been jailed once for security offences, was ordered to leave Northern Ireland by midnight last Saturday because of his opposition to the policies being pursued by the CLMC, which says it is committed to its 23-month truce.
He has refused to leave the province and says he has the support of hardline and moderate Loyalists in his native Portadown, south of Belfast.

Wright has never been convicted of membership of the outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force guerrillas, one of the groups under the CLMC umbrella, but has been linked in the media to leadership of the militia's mid-Ulster group.

If the Loyalist parties were expelled from the talks, it would leave them dominated by mainstream Protestant and Catholic parties who have been unable to reconcile the two communities in a political settlement for almost three decades.
Mayhew acknowledged that the talks, chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, were "maddeningly slow" after months of wrangling over procedure and the setting of an agenda.
They resume in Belfast next Monday faced with the task of deciding when and how they should discuss disarming guerrilla groups, both Protestant and Catholic-backed alike.
The IRA resumed its war on Britain in February because of the British and Irish government's resolve to make disarming guerrillas an agenda item.
The IRA, and some sections of the CLMC, say that disarmament can only be discussed after a political settlement is reached to end 27 years of conflict which killed 3,200.
